items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1967-02-09
items.q: I've seen him ask Duke, come on and sit down and play a little bit. And Duke wouldn't follow that. Duke had his band at the cotton club.

ctx.x: That's right. Well, not the sort of swing you know. Why do you think that Jelly didn't have very much influence on musicians that came after him? Whereas other pianists, like Earl Hines, had tremendous influence on them?

Well, Jelly was a different person from Earl Hines, you see. As I told you, his thinking was different. Jelly was a great musician, but he wasn't commercialized. Jelly had two or three bands, you know what I mean? Coming up in the early 30s. And he just didn't care about going through all these headaches, to build a band, to continue on. He figured his name was there. He was Jelly Roll Morton. He was different. He was just a different, he was a character, as I said. Money didn't mean nothing to Jelly. He was a…
Duke was being quoted as saying that he thought Jelly was a very bad musician.
